# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. Hot take: Joker: Folie à Deux is over-hated because fans can’t stomach that Joker is a loser.

**Score:** 98
**Body:** I find that Joker: Folie à Deux is over-hated because of its musical elements and story direction, but Joaquin Phoenix’s performance as this more down-trodden Joker is underrated and one of the best Jokers in recent memory.

I suspect a lot of the negative reviews for this movie came from fans expecting Joker to triumph, take over the city, and become a more grounded version of comics Joker, and were disappointed with the tragic direction of the film.

To appreciate the direction of Joker: Folie à Deux is to understand that if the Joker were real, he would never become the clown prince of Gotham. Someone like Arthur would likely be crushed by institutions that are indifferent to him, rather than somehow ascending into a supervillain capable of controlling an entire city. In spite of his fandom, he is still a mentally unstable murderer in jail.

The movie's greatest trick is that it refuses to give both Arthur's followers and the audience the Joker they want. Everyone keeps waiting for Arthur to become larger than life, but the movie keeps reducing him back to a frail, mentally unstable, deeply damaged man. When he finally rejects the Joker persona, the people who claimed to love him abandon him. In that sense, Folie à Deux is less interested in asking how the Joker rises than in asking why everyone is so desperate to see him rise in the first place.

It's sad we sweep such a great performance by Phoenix under the rug because people didn't like their Joker fantasy crushed alongside a Gaga soundtrack.

### Top 9 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. This film was a personal attack against everyone who had Arthur Fleck as their lockscreen which was pretty funny. I saw this in theaters and I remember the cinematography being top-tier, and admiring the bold swing of the characterization. I don’t know if I’d ever watch it again because I got really bored and started waiting for it to end, but I appreciate the concept.
  - Todd Phillips is angry with all of his fanboys for not actually "getting" his totally deep and incisive social commentary in Joker, because Todd Phillips is the most insufferable “film bro,” in existence, one who has a shallow understanding of the art that he pilfered from to create the first Joker movie, yet he harbors nothing but seething contempt against his own fanboys for, in turn, having the audacity to fall in love with his monumentally stupid and shallow movie in spite of itself, as if they are the problem here.
2. It’s a boring fucking movie. Doesn’t matter if the Joker is a loser or a god. It’s terrible at executing everything it’s trying to execute.

It has a great thematic concept, actively trying to ruin the love people had for the character. The idea is awesome. Just really shitty how it plays out.

[Thematic breakdown](https://filmcolossus.com/joker-folie-a-deux-explained-2024)
  - 💯. We can make video essays and write about it for years but bottom line is the movie was terrible regardless of what exactly it was trying to tell. I think the joker worship was overblown after the first one too. Just like the hate for women in Star Wars felt like a perfect scapegoat for the garbage the Last Jedi was. Obviously there were incels and neckbeards in both camps but they were also used to push a different narrative 

As someone not remotely that invested in either fandom but hated both these sequels I can tell you it wasn’t because the cast or because I wanted Joker to be my mental health warrior. 

Joker cringe was already a thing years before Joker added to the cringe of obsessing over him.
3. I appreciate the logic of your argument, but as someone who loved Joker 1, but didn't really have a big investment in the character one way or another (I didn't need him to be a winner or a loser...he mostly was a loser in film 1), they just swung incredibly hard in Joker 2 and missed. I guess I can see that it was a reaction to the first film being embraced by political and cultural elements, and big, calculated FU to that. But the truth is, it really did not work...pretty much at all. I wish it did.

Of course, just an opinion. I'm glad you loved it.
4. As someone who 100% agrees with the choices made for Arthur's character... the execution of the film still has major problems. 

The musical numbers begin well but then simply last too long; are too repetitive; don't cut through to Arthur's decaying interior world in sharp fashion. The pacing becomes monotonous and the musical format becomes an albatross around the neck of the film. The expression needed more musical storytelling devices, like arcing from classical musical song and dance numbers to music video to speed-of-streaming song changes which mirror his mental decline.

But the director stuck with the same plodding style and it tests patience.

You are right though, it upset the edgelords. Like The Last Jedi offended the Star Wars nerds.
5. In my opinion, the film doesn't work simply because the writing and directing is just incompetent in bringing the audience on board on whatever they are trying to do. It could be a musical, no problem, and it does look beautiful, but the film creates a huge wall between the story and the audience, and that's the reason it's a massive mistake. The joker can be a loser, and he actually is in the first movie. But this time around he remains the loser and the filmmakers somehow thought it would be interesting to put his character into constant humiliation and pain. What's the payoff on that? There is no payoff. The guy goes into a bad luck spree from minute one up until the final scene. For what? Did they really think people were cheering for the joker and decided to leave no room for mistakes? Maybe, but the final result is a very odd, long and boring movie. And the musical numbers are dull and full of uncreative setups. This is a recipe for a disaster.
6. The few comparisons I’ve seen to The Last Jedi are interesting because I feel like the two films go completely different directions with deconstructing a protagonist.

Both are shown to be deeply flawed but the Last Jedi builds Luke up by reminding the audience that he is, at his core, a hero who will face down an army and be badass enough to win without having to harm a single person, and really makes him out to be the purest reflection of a Jedi we’ve seen.

Joker is shown to be deeply delusional and unworthy of attention but I really don’t feel like it says anything meaningful when it does it. If the entire assertion is that “the joker isn’t worth your sympathy or your time”…why did the first movie spend so much time engaging with him as a person and doing things that were clearly meant to instill sympathy with the character?

It’s worth noting I also don’t like the first Joker either but seeing a movie present a take I don’t like only for the sequel to say how bad that take is just leaves me wondering why I just watched two movies with nothing to say.
7. Similar to my feelings on Matrix 4. They tried to forcibly wake people up and get them to not want the AI steak, but people refused and said, "nah fam, plug me back in - we wanted sequels." Matrix 4 is a bad movie, but it's the most Matrix of the Matrix films. But people just want cool action movie. So AI steak it is.
8. The Joker is a comic book character. Holding the character to realistic outcomes misses the point.

What you’ve said basically reads like “Superman should never save anyone, because if he flew as fast as he does in the comics in real life, the atmosphere would ignite”

There are far better ways to make a villain protagonist unpalatable to the audience than what they did in Joker 2.

## 2. A Gnostic Christian read of The Night of the Hunter (1955)

**Score:** 23
**Body:** Hi all!

I recently watched The Night of the Hunter, and was absolutely amazed by it, as I think anyone would be. I have an interpretation that I suspect is not fully original, nor intended by the creators, maybe not even fully coherent, but I can't stop thinking about it, and want to get it out there, even if just to see some holes poked into it.

**Biblical themes in The Night of the Hunter**

The biblical themes in the movie are obvious. It itself draws a parallel between Pearl and John, and the stories of both Moses, and the killing of the firstborn in Egypt, and King Herod's massacre of the innocents, casting Pearl and John in the role of Moses, and Jesus's family respectively.

Both parallels are drawn by Miss Cooper, who, in many ways, is the polar opposite equivalent of Preacher Powell. However, there are some other biblical themes specifically around the preacher that I believe are less overt, but no less important.

Obviously, by implication of the above parallels, he takes the role of the pharaoh, or King Harod respectfully in the metaphors, both overtly negative figures who kill children. However, in the basement scene, he is also cast, visually, and thematically in the role of Abraham.

I cannot insert images, but if you remember the shot of Powell holding down the head of John, with knife out next to him, while looking up at the sky and talking to God, and are also familiar with artistic depictions of the sacrifice of Isaac by Abraham, such as the Caravaggio painting, the parallels should be obvious. I am drawing attention to this only to show that Preacher Powell is not exclusively cast as negative biblical characters, but also a positive old Testament figure.

**A quick 101 on Gnostic Christianity**

*Disclaimer, this is not a fully comprehensive account of Gnostic beliefs, nor representative of every strain of it, obviously, just a short paragraph of my understanding, that is relevant to this analysis.*

Gnostic Christianity is/was an early sect of the christian faith, today considered heretic by the main christian churches you know. It's primary, and most interesting for us belief is that God, here called Monad, the all powerful, all good being exists, but the world was created not by them, but by a lesser, and evil being called the Demiurge. This is the explanation for the "problem of evil" in Gnosticism. In Gnostic Christianity specifically, the old testament God is this Demiurge, while Jesus is an incarnate or embodiment of the actual supreme being.

**Connecting Gnostic Christianity to The Night of the Hunter**

There are several allusions to Preacher Powell being a Christian, but also not a member of any "official" church. We see him talk to God, and pray when alone, so he is clearly a believer in some form of Christianity, however, he describes his faith, in response to the question "What religion you profess, Preacher?", as "The religion the Almighty and me worked out betwixt us."

Therefore, I posit, that the Preacher is the representative of an archon, a servant of the Demiurge, or is in some other way "on the same side". He is clearly a believer, a man of God, someone who at least takes orders from what he thinks to be the Christian God, but is fundamentally a force of evil, having murdered "twenty-five wives" as we learn towards the very end, in addition to the child murders he tries to commit during the movie.

What I think is my strongest evidence, however, is the opposition/tension between Preacher Powell and Jesus, that doesn't exist between him and God. This makes way stronger sense, I think, in my Gnostic Christian interpretation, where God tells him to kill women, (explicit in the scene where he gets arrested while watching a dance) and at least approves of him killing children, then if he was a "regular" Christian, which we already know he isn't, as he is not a member of any recognized, official church.

This opposition is shown in Powell being condemned at Christmas, the birth of Christ, but way stronger in an earlier scene.

When Powell is sitting outside, waiting for an opportunity to kill or kidnap Pearl and John, with Miss Cooper awake, with a gun, guarding the house, we hear Powell sing the same song he sang in multiple scenes during his pursuit of the kids. The big difference, in this scene, is that Miss Cooper joins in - and we learn, that what Powell sang as "Leaning, Leaning" is actually "Leaning on Jesus, Leaning on Jesus". The following lines, talking about the arms of a higher power the singer is leaning on are present in both versions, but Powell doesn't view Jesus as a representative of that higher power, since he is a servant of the Demiurge, not the higher Gnostic God that Jesus is the embodiment of. I feel this also explains the parallel between Abraham and Preacher Powell, as both, in a Gnostic Christian interpretation, were hearing and following the commands of the Demiurge.

Again, I am not saying this is an intended reading, and I may be placing too much weight on that one singing scene, as it was my favorite from the whole movie overall, even if the famous river scene is a very, very close second.

### Top 2 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. This is one of my favorite films, and I am very interested in Gnosticism, so this was a pleasure to read.

What is your interpretation of the sexual themes in the movie (regardless of whether it relates to Gnosticism or not)? There's a lot going on with the switchblade as a phallic symbol, Powell's shaming of the mother on their wedding night while making her look in the mirror, etc.
  - Thank you! I have to sit on it more, and probably rewatch it before declaring it among my favorites, but it probably will be. I love Béla Tarr, early Lynch, and for a more modern one, Eggers' Lighthouse, so very striking black and white cinematography with a darker story is certainly something right up my alley. Especially Powell is an amazing horror villain, excellently written, and simply perfectly acted.

I don't think it fits particularly well to be fair, not beyond the way any other act of cruelty does. If I really want to stretch it, the way he talks to the mother on the wedding night could be this hatred and evil towards the human species and human sexuality that comes from the Demiurge that you also see in the old testament's vengeful God?

Feels like the closest thing for me right now, as that element of sex and being sexually attractive being inherently sinful and disgusting, except when for reproduction, is very much an element of the Old Testament's God, aka the Demiurge. It feels like much more of a stretch then the Jesus and Abraham parts to me, but it does fit.
2. Harry Powell represents a modern-day deceiver. He's that what Apostle Paul called the outlaw, the lawless one, the *anomos*.

Indeed, you can recognize several Biblical themes across the film, but I'm not so sure about Gnosticism. Gnosticism is all about mythologizing Christianism by a strange juxtaposition of Neo-Platonism and Neo-Pitagorism. It offers a maze-like framework of redemption, yet human souls remain passive as agents. Enduring the broken link between God and the Demiurge, although acting according the gnosis.

On the contrary, Harry Powell is all about the material world. There's no higher planes of existence, but power-driven transactions. In order to fulfill his corrupted deed, he lures people by misusing the word of God. He's not only a silver tongue devil; also, he brings ruin and demise, just as 2 Thessalonians 2:8 warns.
  - This is some "From Hell" level esoteric shit. Thanks for sharing!

## 3. Wake In Fright (1971): drunkeness on film

**Score:** 20
**Body:** Synopsis via IMDB:

After a bad gambling bet, a schoolteacher is marooned in a town full of crazy, drunk, violent men who threaten to make him just as crazy, drunk, and violent.

Ted Kotcheff's 1971 film, based on the novel of the same name by Evan Jones, was a box-office flop despite a good critical reception. Set in the Australian Outback and featuring many local non-actors, it is a frank portrait of the hypermasculine, hard-drinking culture of the region. For this reason, many members of the Australian public were unhappy with how their country was portrayed in the film. Due in no small part to its financial failure, the film was almost lost forever, only to be rediscovered decades later.

There's a lot to say about rural isolation and masculinity in this film, but I want to focus on its portrayl of drunkeness. It seems to capture the feeling of being absolutely shitfaced without relying too heavily on cheap tricks like spinning camera movements. There is one particular sequence where the main character, played by Gary Bond, blacks out and reawakens that feels very authentic.

Drunk acting is also a highlight here, especially in Donald Pleasants' performance as the alcoholic doctor. There is something particularly tragic about an obviously intelligent man who has given into his basest instincts and descended into substance abuse>!although his implied rape of the protagonist makes him less sympathetic to be sure.!<

I remember seeing a funny Instagram skit about how writers of movies and tv shows often seem to have no idea what its like to be drunk or hungover. This is certainly not the case for Wake In Fright. The hangover scenes are realistic to the point of being physically sickening. And even when the drinking buddies' roughousing degenerates into a destructive brawl, there is little exaggeration at play. ## 5. Diary of a Country Preist - God's Face

**Score:** 3
**Body:** Does he see it? We can't know, like many other things we can't know about in this elusive film.

The sense of mystery keeps us engaged. The state of transcendence we feel we are about to attain, the reward.

The cadence he maintains, knowing when to speed it up or slow it down, is all just too perfect. This movie is perfect. 

It's too beautiful to be deflating despite the bleakness of the story, and the austerity of the cinematography. I was blown away at the end of it, but one has to think what was it all for?
